name: Ballot order effect
statement: Candidates listed first on a ballot are said to gain votes for that reason alone, by more where voters know least about the race.
meaning: This is the serial position effect measured in vote counts rather than in a laboratory. Several jurisdictions rotate or randomise the order of candidate names across voting places, so the same candidate is printed first for some voters and later for others. The difference in vote share between those groups is the estimate. MacInnis and colleagues set out two psychological accounts of why the difference is not zero. A voter asked to decide a race they know nothing about is pulled towards the option they consider first. A voter who does know something searches memory for reasons to support each name in turn, and generates fewer supporting thoughts as attention flags, which favours the names read early. Both accounts predict the same moderator, and it is the moderator that carries most of the interest here: the less information a race supplies, the more the first slot is worth.

origin.who: Joanne M. Miller and Jon A. Krosnick
origin.note: Their study of the 1992 Ohio elections set the modern template of testing name order against rotated ballots. Ballot position research is much older. Ho and Imai date current interest to half a century of work and cite Gold in 1952 and Bain and Hecock's 1957 book Ballot Position and Voter's Choice; MacInnis and colleagues cite a study of the 1920 Pennsylvania primary.

evidence:
California has drawn a randomised alphabet from a lottery container since 1975 and rotates the resulting order through its 80 assembly districts. Ho and Imai treated that as a natural experiment covering 473 candidates in 80 statewide races between 1978 and 2002, 37,840 district-race observations in all. In general elections the major parties gained nothing from first position: 0.05 percentage points for Democrats with a standard error of 0.46, and -0.06 points for Republicans with a standard error of 0.53. In primaries the same parties gained 1.89 points (SE 0.32) and 2.16 points (SE 0.46). Nonpartisan candidates gained 1.95 points in general elections and 3.44 in primaries, and minor parties in primaries gained more still, 6.59 points for the Libertarians and 6.31 for Peace and Freedom. Across the 1998 and 2000 general elections the median candidate gain was about 0.2 points, and every statistically significant positive effect belonged to a minor party or a nonpartisan candidate. Across the same years' primaries the median was about 1.6 points. In 7 of 59 primary races the estimated advantage was positive and possibly greater than the winner's margin, which Ho and Imai read as ballot order having potentially changed the result in as many as 12% of the primaries they examined.

Meredith and Salant asked who takes the seat rather than what happens to vote shares. In California city council and school board elections, candidates listed first win office between four and five percentage points more often than expected without order effects, which the authors gloss as winning roughly one election in ten that they would otherwise lose. The loss falls on candidates in the median ballot position, who win two to three points less often than expected. The advantage was larger in races with more candidates, and was not distinguishable between city council and school board races, open and incumbent races, or consolidated and standalone elections. Those figures are read off the authors' working-paper version of the paper published in Political Behavior in 2013.

Three further jurisdictions come at one remove, through MacInnis and colleagues' summary of them rather than the papers themselves. In the three largest Ohio counties in 1992, Miller and Krosnick found 86% of 196 name-order tests pointing towards primacy, statistically significant effects in 48% of races, and those significant effects averaging 2.33 percentage points. In the 1998 Democratic primary in New York City, Koppell and Steen found first listing worth more votes for 89% of 180 candidates, with effects that were significant or marginally so in 21 of 79 races, averaging 6.86 points and reaching 11.30. In the 2014 Texas primaries, Grant found every candidate showing a primacy effect and every effect statistically significant, averaging 5.32 points with a maximum of 10.48. Grant's own summary of that work puts the gain from moving from last to first at nearly ten percentage points in down-ballot and judicial contests, and reports no such gain in the high-profile races.

replication.headline: Primacy appeared in 86% of 84 name-order tests in New Hampshire, a state chosen because high turnout and party column ballots should have suppressed it.
replication.detail: MacInnis, Miller, Krosnick, Below and Lindner analysed name rotations across New Hampshire's 323 voting places, covering the 2000, 2002 and 2004 primaries and the 2012 and 2016 general elections. Of 51 primary analyses, 90% ran in the direction of primacy, against the 50% expected by chance, with a sign test at p < .001. Of those, 41% reached statistical significance, ranging from 0.3 to 7.1 percentage points and averaging 2.8. Of 33 general election candidates, 67% ran towards primacy, p < .04, and the significant effects averaged 1.1 points. In the 2016 presidential race Donald Trump gained 1.7 points from first listing (p = .049) and Hillary Clinton 1.5 (p = .071), pooling to 1.6 points (p = .028). The moderators held. Primary candidates showed effects 1.89 points larger than non-major-party candidates in general elections (SE 0.42), the effect in the most publicised contest was 2.42 points smaller than in the least publicised (SE 1.01), and contests with an incumbent running were 1.06 points lower (SE 0.53). With all moderators entered together the publicity coefficient lost statistical significance and the margin-of-victory coefficient fell to near zero.

study.cite: MacInnis, B., Miller, J. M., Krosnick, J. A., Below, C., & Lindner, M. (2021). Candidate name order effects in New Hampshire: Evidence from primaries and from general elections with party column ballots. PLOS ONE, 16(3), e0248049.

limits:
No structured effect sizes are printed above, and that is the finding rather than a gap. No meta-analysis or systematic review of ballot order effects was located, and the estimates below come from separate jurisdictions using different designs, different outcomes and different denominators. A single pooled number would hide the thing worth knowing: the gain to first position runs from about a fifth of a percentage point among major-party candidates in publicised general elections to something near ten points in down-ballot primaries and judicial races. The Ohio, New York City and Texas figures above are quoted through MacInnis and colleagues and not off the original papers, so they stay out of the structured fields.

The evidence base is also narrow geographically. The quasi-experiments require a jurisdiction that rotates or randomises order, which in practice has meant California, Ohio, North Dakota, New Hampshire, New York City, Texas and Illinois. Ho and Imai list their own constraints: statewide races only, so smaller local races where cognitive costs are higher are outside the data; California publicises its randomisation, so voters aware of it may behave differently; and only 80 assembly districts supply the variation, which is few outcomes per ballot position. Their data contain one nonpartisan office, Superintendent of Public Instruction, so the large nonpartisan effect cannot be separated from that office's obscurity. Their own paper is not quite consistent on that figure: the abstract puts the nonpartisan gain at three percentage points, the introduction at two, and Table 4 gives 1.95 in general elections and 3.44 in primaries.

There is a live dispute about general elections. Ho and Imai report no detectable effect for major-party candidates there and attribute earlier large estimates to confounding, multiple testing and parametric assumptions. Pasek and colleagues, analysing 402 candidates in California general elections from 1976 to 2006, report a consistent though modest primacy effect, and MacInnis and colleagues argue that Ho and Imai's data contained entry errors and lacked controls for the party registration of assembly districts. Nothing in that dispute touches primaries and low-information races, where the two camps agree.
misreadings:
Quoting one average for the ballot order effect misrepresents it. The number is not a constant of psychology but a function of how much else the voter has to go on, and the same study can produce a null for a presidential race and six points for a minor-party primary candidate. Reform arguments that carry a single figure across all races are using the wrong one somewhere.

The largest figures in circulation are the least secure. Krosnick, Miller and Tichy reported that first listing raised George W. Bush's vote share in California in 2000 by about nine and a half percentage points against last listing. Ho and Imai reproduce that estimate at 9.45 points and then show that Republican registration rates by ballot place trace almost the same curve, correlating with vote shares at 0.98, so the pattern is partisanship rather than position. Using all districts instead of first against last, the difference falls to roughly one point and stops being statistically significant. An older figure has had a longer life: Ho and Imai note that Scott's 1972 study of ten California races concluded that at least five percentage points of the first-listed candidate's vote could be attributed to position, and that the California Secretary of State has quoted it since.

An effect on vote share is not the same claim as an effect on who wins, and the two are often run together. Ho and Imai found no conclusive evidence of an effect on major candidates in general elections even where races were close. Meredith and Salant list the counts of races where the estimated advantage exceeded the winning margin: four of the 118 elections in Miller and Krosnick, seven of Koppell and Steen's 79 contests, seven of Ho and Imai's 59, and 40 of the 595 races King and Leigh studied in Australia. They also point out that such counts overstate the change in representation, since the first-listed candidate has to be the one who won. In King and Leigh's 40 races the winner was listed first in five.
